la:adj:multus.html:
multus (old form moltus), a, um;
comp. plus; sup. plurimus (v. at the end of this art.), adj.
etym. dub.
, much, great, many, of things corporeal and incorporeal.
Posit.
In gen.: multi mortales, Cato ap. : multi suam rem

bene gessere: multi qui, etc., Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 295 sq. Vahl.): multi fortissimi viri,: rationes,. tam multis verbis scribere, at such length, : beneficia. Cato ap. Fest. s. v. ratissima, p. 286 Müll.: multi alii,.—When used with another adjective it is usually connected with it by a conjunction: multae et magnae contentiones,many great conlests,; : O multas et graves offensiones,: multi et graves dolores,: multi et varii timores,: multae bonaeque artes animi,: multa et clara facinora,.—But when the second adjective is used substantively the conjunction is omitted: multi improbi,; : multi boni, docti, prudentes,: multi nobiles,: multa acerba habuit ille annus,; : multa infanda,: multa falsa,.—Also, when the second adjective forms with its substantive a single conception: multa secunda proelia,victories,; ; : multa libera capita,freemen,: multae liberae civitates,republics,: multos fortes viros,; : multi clari viri,noblemen,: multi primarii viri,.—Similarly, et is omitted between multi and adjectives which form with their substantives familiar phrases: multi clarissimi viri,: multi amplissimi viri,; ; ; ; ; : multi honestissimi homines,: multi peritissimi homines,: multi summi homines,; : multi clarissimi et sapientissimi viri,; .—Et is also omitted when the substantive stands between the two adjectives: in veteribus patronis multis,: multa praeterea bella gravia,: multis suppliciis justis,: multa majores nostri magna et gravia bella gesserunt,: plurima signa pulcherrima,.—When both adjectives follow the substantive, et is sometimes inserted: virtutes animi multae et magnae,: causas ille multas et graves habuit,; and is sometimes omitted, the emphasis then falling on the second adjective: utebatur hominibus improbis, multis,: prodigia multa, foeda,.—With a partitive gen.: multi hominum,: multae silvestrium arborum,.—In neutr. plur.: multa, ōrum, many things, much: nimium multa,: nimis multa,: insulae non ita multae,not so many, not so very many,: parum multa scire,too few,: bene multi, a good many, Asin. ap. : quam minime multa vestigia servitutis,as few as possible,: minime multi remiges,exceedingly few,: in multas pecunias alienissimorum hominum invasit,; : multae pecuniae variis ex causis a privatis detinentur,.—Sometimes multi stands for multi alii, many others: nam certe Pompeio, et a Curionibus patre et filio, et a multis exprobratum est,.—The sing. also is used poet. for the plur., many a: aut trudit acres hinc et hinc multā cane Apros in obstantes plagas,with many dogs,: multa prece prosequi,: multā victima,: agna. : avis,: tabella,; so of persons: multus sua vulnera puppi Affixit moriens, many a one, for multi affixerunt, .—In sing., to denote quantity, much, great, abundant: multum aurum et argentum. ; : exstructa mensa multā carne rancidā,: multo labore quaerere aliquid,with much labor, great exertion,: cura,: sol,much sun,: sermo, much conversalion, Brut. ap. : stilus tuus multi sudoris est. : multo cibo et potione completi, id. Tusc. 5, 35, 100: multo sanguine ea Poenis victoria stetit,: multum sanguinem haurire,; : multam harenam mare evomit,: arbor,: silva,: multae vestis injectu opprimi,: multa et lauta supellex,: aurum,; ; ; : libertas,: multam salutem dicere alicui,to greet heartily,: cum auro et argento multo,.—Of time: Itaque multum diei processerat,a great part of the day,: ad multum diem,till far in the day,: multo adhuc die,when much of the day was still remaining, when it was still high day,: multo denique die,when the day was far spent,: multā nocte,late at night,: multo mane,very early,: multa opinio, for multorum,the general opinion,: velut multā pace,as in a general peace, as if there were peace everywhere,: multus homo,one who gives himself up to the lusts of many,.—multi, ōrum, m., the many, the common mass, the multitude: probis probatus potius, quam multis forem, Att. ap. : video ego te, mulier, more multarum utier,—Esp.: unus e (or de) multis, one of the multitude, a man of no distinction: tenuis L. Virginius unusque e multis,: unus de multis esse,: M. Calidius non fuit orator unus e multis; potius inter multos prope singularis fuit,: numerarer in multis,among the herd of orators,: e multis una sit tibi,no better than others,: multum est,it is of importance,.—In neutr. absol.: ne multa, or ne multis, not to be prolix, in short: ne multa: perquiritur a coactoribus,: ne multis: Diogenes emitur,: quid multis moror?.—Sometimes multa is used (particularly by the poets) adverbially, much, greatly, very: multa reluctari,: gemens,; : deos testatus,: invehi, (cf. nonnulla invehi, ): haud multa moratus,.—Rarely in multum: in multum velociores,by far,.—

In partic.
Too much, overmuch, excessive: supellex modica, non multa,.—
In speech, much-speaking, diffuse, prolix: qui in aliquo genere aut inconcinnus aut multus est,: ne in re notā et pervulgatā multus et insolens sim,: nolo in stellarum ratione multus vobis videri,.—
Frequent, frequently present: in operibus, in agmine, atque ad vigilias multus adesse,: multus in eo proelio Caesar fuit,was in many places,: hen hercle hominem multum et odiosum mihi!troublesome, tedious,: instare,.—Hence, adv., in two forms.
multum, much, very much, greatly, very, often, frequently, far, etc. (class.): salve multum, gnate mi,: multum vale,farewell,: hominem ineptum multum et odiosum mihi,: opinor, Cassium uti non ita multum sorore,not very much,: multum mecum municipales homines loquuntur,often,: non multum ille quidem nec saepe dicebat,: non multum confidere,not very much, not particularly,: sunt in venationibus,often, frequently,: in eodem genere causarum multum erat T. Juventius,: multum fuisse cum aliquo,to have had much intercourse with,: sum multum equidem cum Phaedro in Epicuri hortis,: gratiā valere,to be in great favor,: res multum et saepe quaesita,: longe omnes multumque superabit,: multum et diu cogitans,: diu multumque scriptitare,.—With an adj.: multum loquaces,very talkative,: mepti labores,very,.—Poet. also with comp.: multum improbiores sunt quam a primo credidi,much, far,: multum robustior illo,: majora,.— So with infra, post: haud multum infra viam,; : haud multum post mortem ejus,: ut multum,at most,; .—
multōby much, much, a great deal, far, by far (class.).
With comparatives and verbs which imply comparison: multo tanto carior,: pauciores oratores,: facilius atque expeditius iter,.—With verbs: virtutem omnibus rebus multo anteponentes,: multo ceteros anteibant,: multo praestat beneficii, quam maleficii immemorem esse,.—With malle: multo mavolo,; : meo judicio multo stare malo, quam, etc.,.—
With sup. (rare but class.), by far, by much: quae tibi mulier videtur multo sapientissuma,; : multo optimus hostis, by far, Lucil. ap. : simulacrum multo antiquissimum,; ; : maxima pars,; cf. : multo id bellum maximum fuit,: pars multo maxima,: multo molestissima, : multo gratissima lux,: foedissimum,: optimum,: pulcherrimum,: utilissima,: maxime,: multo maxime miserabile,: multo maxime ingenio validus,.—
With particles denoting a difference, far, greatly, very: multo aliter,: multo aliter ac sperabat,far otherwise than,: quod non multo secus fieret, si,not far otherwise, not very different,: multo infra Cyrenaicum. . —
In specifications of time, before ante and post, long, much: non multo ante urbem captam,: non multo ante,not long before,: multo ante,: non multo post, quam, etc.,not long after,: haud multo ante solis occasum,: multo ante noctem,.—
Very rarely with the positive for multum: maligna multo,very, Umpf.—
Doubled, multo multoque, with comparatives: multo multoque longior,far, very much,: multo multoque operosius est,: multo multoque magis, Front. Laud. Negl. § 3.
Comp.: plūs, plūris; in the plur., plūres, plūra (in sing. anciently written plous; three times in the S. C. de Bacch. Here perh. belongs, in the plur., pleores and pleoris, for plures, in the Song of the Arval Brothers.—For the class. neuter of the plur., plura, the form pluria was used in ante-class. Latinity. Gellius cites M. Cato, Q. Claudius, Valerius Antias, L. Ælius, P. Nigidius, and M. Varro as authorities for this form, ; yet Plautus and Terence have only plura; and the earlier reading pluria, in ; ; , is now supplanted by the critically certain plura and plurima.—The gen. plur. plurium, however, has remained the predominant form, e. g. ; ; et saep.) [from the root ple; Gr. πλέον, πίμπλημι; cf. plenus, plera, compleo, etc.; also locu-ples, plebes, populus, etc.], more.
In the sing. (used both substantively and adverbially): LIBRAS FARRIS ENDO DIES DATO. SI VOLET PLVS DATO, Fragm. XII. Tab. in : SI PLVS MINVSVE SECVERVNT, SE FRAVDE ESTO, ib.; so (perh. in imitation of this legal phrase): ebeu, cur ego plus minusve feci quam aequom fuit!; : ne plus minusve loqueretur,; cf. ; and in the signif. of circiter, about: septingenti sunt paulo plus aut minus anni ... postquam, etc., Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 493 Vahl.); so. non longius abesse plus minus octo milibus, Oud.; cf.: speranti plures ... venerunt plusve minusve duae,: aut ne quid faciam plus, quod post me minus fecisse satius sit,too much ... too little,: tantum et plus etiam ipse mihi deberet,: vos et decem numero, et, quod plus est, Romani estis,and what is more,: verbane plus an sententia valere debeat,:

cf.: apud me argumenta plus quam testes valent,: valet enim salus plus quam libido,.—

With a partitive gen.: vultis pecuniae plus habere,; cf.: nostri casus plus honoris habuerunt quam laboris,; so, plus virium,: plus hostium,: plus dapis et rixae multo minus invidiaeque,: in hac causā eo plus auctoritatis habent, quia, etc.,; cf.: plus ingenii,: Albano non plus animi erat quam fidei,as little courage as fidelity,.—
With quam (some examples of which have already been given above): non plus quam semel,: confiteor eos ... plus quam sicarios esse,: ne plus reddat quam acceperit, et saep.: non plus quam in tres partis posse distribui putaverunt,into not more than,: plus quam decem dies abesse,: nulla (navis) plus quam triginta remis agatur,with more than,.—
Without quam: HOMINES PLOVS V. OINVORSEI VIREI ATQVE MVLIERES, S. C. de Bacch. 19 (Wordsw. Fragm. and Spec. p. 173): plus mille capti,: plus milies audivi,: plus semel, Varr. ap. : plus quingentos colaphos infregit mihi,: ferre plus dimidiati mensis cibaria,: non plus mille quingentos aeris,: paulo plus ducentos passus a castris,: cum plus annum aeger fuisset,: parte plus dimidiā rem auctam,.—(ε) With a compar. or adverbial abl., or with an abl. of measure: VIREI PLOVS DVOBVS, S. C. de Bacch. 20 (Wordsw. Fragm. and Spec. p. 173): de paupertate tacentes Plus poscente ferent,more than the importunate,: ex his alius alio plus habet virium,: cave putes hoc tempore plus me quemquam cruciari, Balb. ap. , A, 2: alterum certe non potest, ut plus una vera sit,; cf.: in columbā plures videri colores, nec esse plus uno,: HOC PLVS NE FACITO, more than this, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. : annos sexaginta natus es Aut plus eo,or more than that,: plus aequo,: plus paulo,: paulo plus,: multo plus, Anton. ap. , A, 1: plus nimio,overmuch,: quam molestum est uno digito plus habere, too much by a finger, i. e. a finger too much, : uno plus Etruscorum cecidisse in acie,one man more,.—
In the gen. pretii, pluris, of more value, of a higher price, for more, higher, dearer: ut plus reddant musti et olei, et pretii pluris,of greater value,: ager multo pluris est,is worth much more,; cf.: quo pluris sint nostra oliveta,: pluris emere,dearer,; so, vendere,; ; : aedificare,: pluris est oculatus testis quam auriti decem,of more value,: mea mihi conscientia pluris est, quam omnium sermo,: facio pluris omnium hominem neminem,: facere aliquem pluris,make more of one, esteem him more highly,: pluris habere,: aestimare,: ducere,: putare, et saep.—
Rarely, instead of the genitive, in the abl. pretii: plure vendunt, Lucil. ap. P.: plure altero tanto, quanto ejus fundus est, velim, Plaut. ib.: plure venit, Cic. ib.—
Plus plusque, more and more: quem mehercule plus plusque in dies diligo. .—*
Like magis, with an adj.: plus formosus, for formosior,.—
In the plur.
Comparatively, more in number: omnes qui aere alieno premantur, quos plures esse intellego quam putāram,; : nemini ego plura acerba esse credo ex amore homini umquam oblata quam mihi,: ne plura insignia essent imperii in libero populo quam in regno fuissent,: multo plura,many more things,.—
In gen., of a great number, many: qui plus fore dicant in pluribus consilii quam in uno. : cf.: quid quaeso interest inter unum et plures, si justitia est in pluribus? ; 1, 34, 52: non possunt unā in civitate multi rem ac fortunas amittere, ut non plures secum in eandem trahant calamitatem,: quod pluribus praesentibus eas res jactari nolebat,: plura castella Pompeius tentaverat,: summus dolor plures dies manere non potest,: pluribus diebus, Quint. prooem. § 7: illic plurium rerum est congeries,: quae consuetudo sit, pluribus verbis docere,: eum pluribus verbis rogat, ut, etc.,; without verba: quid ego plura dicam?: pluribus haec exsecutus sum,; also elliptically, quid plura? and, ne plura, like quid multa? and ne multa: hic sacra, hic genus, hic majorum multa vestigia. Quid plura? hanc vides villam, etc.,what need of many words? in short,: sed—ne plura—dicendum enim aliquando est—Pomponium Atticum sic amo, ut alterum fratrem,.—
Esp.: plures.
The mass, the multitude, opp. pauciores, = οἱ ὀλίγοι, .—
Euphemistically, acc. to the Gr. οἱ πλείονες, the dead: quin prius Me ad plures penetravi?.—
The greater number, the majority: plures nesciebant quā ex causā convenissent,.
Sup.: plūrĭmus (archaic form, plisima plurima, Paul. ex and 205 Müll.: PLIOIRVME (I), Epit. of Scipio), a, um [from root ple; whence also plus, q. v., ploirumus for ploisumus; and thence the predominant form plurimus], most, very much, or many (as an adj. in good prose mostly in the plur., except the standing formula of greeting: salutem plurimam dicere alicui; v.infra): hujus sunt plurima simulacra,: nos plurimis ignotissimi gentibus,: plurimae et maximae partes,: plurimorum seculorum memoria,: haec plurimis a me verbis dicta sunt, et saep.—In sing.: me plurimā praedā onustum,: sermo,: risus,: res,: exercitatio,: mons,very large,: cervix,: Aetna,.—Of a greeting: impertit salutem plurimam, Lucil. ap. . 16; and esp. freq.: salutem plurimam dicit (commonly abbrev. S. P. D.) at the beginning of letters; v. salus.— Poet.: medio cum plurimus orbe Sol erat,very powerful, oppressive,: plurima quā silva est. thickest, : coma plurima,very thick,: sed plurima nantis in ore Alcyone conjux,mostly, chiefly,.—And collect.: plurimus in Junonis honorem Aptum dicet equis Argos,many a one, very many,; so, oleaster plurimus,: quā plurima mittitur ales,: plurima lecta rosa est,.— In neutr. absol. (substant. or adverb.): ut haberet quam plurimum,as much as possible,: caput autem est, quam plurimum scribere,: ut in quoque oratore plurimum esset,.—Adv.: plūrĭmum: et is valebat in suffragio plurimum, cujus plurimum intererat, esse in optimo statu civitatem,: auspiciis plurimum obsecutus est Romulus,: si vero populus plurimum potest,; cf.: qui apud me dignitate plurimum possunt,: plurimum aliis praestare,: ut te plurimum diligam,; : hoc ego utor uno omnium plurimum,: quantum (al. quanto) plurimum possunt,: plurimum quantum also signifies very much indeed, exceedingly (post-class.): plurimum quantum veritati nocuere,: gratulor,: (elleborum) ex aquā datur plurimum drachma,at the most,; ; ; so, cum plurimum, (opp. to cum minimum); 18, 7, 10, § 60: nec tam numerosa differentia; tribus ut plurimum bonitatibus distat, for the most part, commonly, usually, = plerumque, .—
In neutr. with a partit. gen.: sententiarum et gravitatis plurimum, 1, 18, 25: artis,: auctoritatis et ponderis,: ut laboris sic utilitatis etiam longe plurimum,: virtutum, plurimum quantum favoris partibus dabat fratermtas ducum, .—
In the gen. pretii: plurimi: immo unice unum plurimi pendit,values very highly, esteems very much,: quem unum Alexander plurimi fecerat,: ut quisque quod plurimi est possidet,.

la:noun:multa.html:
multa (mulcta), ae, f.
Sabine, acc. to Varr. ap. ; Oscan, acc. to Paul. ex Müll.
,
a penalty involving loss of property, a fine, amercement, mulct; in the most ancient times riches consisted only in the possession of flocks and herds; it accordingly signified, at first, a fine in cattle; but in later times, when money was the measure of wealth, it signified a pecuniary fine (whereas poena denotes a punishment of any kind, e. g. corporal punishment, imprisonment, capital punishment): vocabulum ipsum multae M. Varro non Latinum, sed Sabinum esse dicit,: multam Osce dici putant poenam quidam. M. Varro ait poenam esse, sed pecuniariam, Paul. ex Mull.: cum pecore diceretur multa, Müll. The highest penalty in the earliest times was thirty head of cattle, the lowest a sheep, in specifying which the word ovis is used as of the masculine gender: ego ei unum ovem multam dico, I condemn him to pay, fine him, a legal formula ap. : multae dictio ovium et bovium,.—Later, of a pecuniary fine: multa praesens quingentum milium aeris in singulas civitates imposita,: multam alicui dicere,to decree, award,: indicere,: subire,: committere,to deserve, incur,: exigere, Müll.: remittere,: irrogare (of the plaintiff, or people's tribune),to propose that the accused be fined a certain sum,; so, petere,: aliquem multā et poenā multare,: multam alicui facere,: certare, to contend on both sides whether or not the proposed fine should be paid: duo tribuni plebis ducentum milium aeris multam M. Postumio dixerunt: cui certandae cum dies advenisset,: multae certatio,: multa erat Veneri,for the benefit of Venus,: multa gravis praedibus Valerianis,a heavy loss, great damage,.—
In gen., a penalty: singulos jure jurando adigam non aliter quam stantes cibum capturos esse ... hanc multam feretis, etc.,: haec ei multa esto: vino viginti dies Ut careat,.

la:verb:multo.gloss: to punish, to sentence, to fine
senses: to punish, to sentence, to fine
la:verb:multo.html:
multo (less correctly mulcto), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
1. multa
,
to punish one with any thing; used mostly of judicial punishment (class.; cf.: punio, animadverto): accusatorem multā et poenā multavit,: vitia hominum atque fraudes damnis, ignominiis, vinculis, verberibus, exsiliis, morte multantur,: imperatorem deminutione provinciae,.—With abl. of that with respect to which the punishment is inflicted: populos stipendio,to sentence them to pay,: exsules bonis,: aliquem pecuniā,to fine in a sum of money,: agris,: Antiochum Asiā,: sacerdotio,: publice armis multati privatis copiis juvere militem,: poculo multabitur,: aliquem votis (like damnare votis), lit., to punish with his vows, i. e. by granting the object of his vows, Naev. ap. : cum ab ipsā fortunā videat hujus consilia esse multata,: boves iniquitate operis (al. mulcare),to torment,.—With dat. of the person for whose benefit: Veneri esse multatum, (in , Ritschl reads mulcaverit, but this seems to be corrupt; v. Ritschl ad h. l.).

la:adv:multo.gloss: by much, much, by far; far, long
senses: by much, much, by far; far, long

la:verb:muto.html:
mūto, āvi, ātum (arch.
subj. mutassis, ; inf. pass. mutarier, ), 1, v. a. and n.freq. [moveo].
Prop., to move, to move away or from its place, to move to a place (rare): neque se luna quoquam mutat,does not move, does not budge,: illa tamen se Non habitu mutatve loco, does not quit her dress or her dwelling, : ne quis invitus civitate mutetur,be forced to leave, be driven from,: hinc dum muter,if I can only get away from here,.—
Transf.
Of change in the thing spoken of itself.
In gen.
Act., to alter, change a thing (freq. and class.; cf. vario): sententiam mutare numquam,: ego rogatus mutavi consilium meum. : consuetudinem dicendi,: mentes vestras voluntatesque,: cum testamentum mutare cuperet,: propositum. : ne haec mutet fidem,: nequeo exorare

ut me maneat et cum illo ut mutet fidem, : tabulas,to alter one's will,.—Absol.: natura nescia mutari,incapable of change,. —With ob: mutatum jus ob unius feneratoris libidinem,: facilem mutatu gentem,.—With ad: gubernatori ad incursus tempestatum ... ratio mutanda est,: ad singulas paene distinctiones vultus mutandus est,.—With Gr. acc.: mutata suos flumina cursus,: negat quicquam ex Latinā ratione mutandum,.—With cum: cum illo fidem, supra; more freq. cum aliquā re, to change with or under the influence of a thing: facies locorum cum ventis simul mutatur,: qui cum fortunā non animum mutāsset,: quarum uvarum vini jucunditas cum regione mutatur,; .—With in and acc.: bona facile mutantur in pejus,.—With ex: nisi forte non ex Graeco mutantes, etc.,: ex feminis mutari in mares,. —With de: de uxore nihil mutat,.—With ab: quantum mutatus ab illo Hectore,: longe mutatus ab illo Sampsone, qui, etc.,, prol. § 13.—Non mutat, with rel.-clause, it makes no difference: nec mutat confestim, an interjecto tempore, fidem suam adstrinxerunt, Pap. . —With abl. instrum. (poet.): ut silvae foliis pronos mutantur in annos,.—

Neutr., = mutari, to alter, change: quantum mores mutaverint argumentum,: postquam mutabat aestus,; : annona ex ante convectā copiā nihil mutavit,: mox in superbiam mutans,: adeo animi mutaverant, ut clariorem inter Romanos deditio Postumium ... faceret,: tantum mutāsse fortunam, ut, etc.,; .—
To differ, be different: pastiones hiberno ac verno tempore hoc mutant,: quantum mutare a Menandro Caecilius visus est,.—
Of style, to vary: an ego ... poetis, et maxime tragicis concederem, ut ne omnibus locis eādem contentione uterentur, crebroque mutarent? etc.,.—
In partic.
To change the color of, to color, dye (cf.: inficio, imbuo): aries jam suave rubenti Murice, jam croceo mutabit vellera luto,: nec lanarum colores, quibus simplex ille candor mutatus est, elui possunt,.—
To change for the better, make better, to improve: placet tibi factum, Micio? Mi.: non, si queam mutare,.—
To change for the worse; pass., of wine, to spoil, turn, etc.: ac, nisi mutatum, parcit defundere vinum,: melle mutatum (sc. balsamum),adulterated,.—
Of change in its relation to other things, etc.
In gen., to change one thing, etc., for another: mutatis ad celeritatem jumentis,: vestimenta mutanti tunica ardere visa est,: calceos et vestimenta,.—Esp. freq.: mutare vestem, to change one's dress: An. Muta vestem. Ch. Ubi mutem? ... An. Eamus ad me. Ibi proximum'st ubi mutes, sqq.: mutando nunc vestem, nunc tegumenta capitis,; .—Esp., to put on the garb of mourning, of humility, etc.: pro me praesente senatus hominumque praeterea viginti millia vestem mutaverunt,: non modo ut vestem mutaret, aut supplex prensaret homines, sed, etc.,; ; ; .—
Esp.
Mutata verba, i. e. figurative: mutata (verba), in quibus pro verbo proprio subicitur aliud, quod idem significet, sumptum ex re aliquā consequenti,.—
Of style, to vary, alter: reliquum est ut dicas de conversā oratione atque mutatā,: genus eloquendi ... mutatum,.—
Of one's assertion or promise: quod dixi semel, hau mutabo,will not break my word,.—
Of place, to change, shift, alter: locum ex loco mutans (sc. typhon) rapidā vertigine,; cf.: quod nec injussu populi mutari finibus posset, to be removed, : exsules sunt, etiam si solum non mutārunt,i. e. gone into exile,: jussa pars mutare Lares et urbem Sospite cursu,.—
Of common or reciprocal relations, to interchange, exchange.—With cum: cum amplificatione vectigalium nomen Hieronicae legis mutare,: ut vestem cum illo mutem,: ne cujus suorum popularium mutatam secum fortunam esse vellent,.—With pro: C. Hostilio pro Etruriā Tarentum mutaverant (sonatus) provinciam, pro Tarento Capuam mutaverunt,: non debere eum incerta pro certis mutare,: mutatos pro Macedonibus Romanos dominos,.—With abl. of that for which the exchange, etc., is made: quid terras alio calentes Sole mutamus (patriā),: victoriae possessionem incertā pace mutāsse,; also with abl. of that given in exchange, etc.: victrice patriā victam mutari,.—So esp. of trading, etc., to exchange, barter, sell, etc.: coepit captivos conmercari Aleos, si quem reperire possit, qui mutet suum,; cf.: homines captivos conmercatur, si queat Aliquem invenire, suum qui mutet filium,; 1, 2, 68: hic mutat merces surgente a sole, etc.,: mutandi copia,.—With abl.: uvam Furtivā mutat strigili,: suburbanis lactens porcus aere mutandus est,: caetera reponantur, vel aere mutentur,: aere mutandi sunt (sc. apri),: quamvis Milesia magno Vellera mutentur,; so with cum and pers. with whom the exchange is made: eaque mutare cum mercatoribus vino advecticio,.—With inter: mutare res inter se instituerant,.—
To forsake, abandon, leave: mutare, derelinquere,: expertum jam principem anxii mutabant,: mihi non persuadetur ... mutem meos, Lucil. ap. : mutataque sidera pondus Quaesivere suum, i. e. forsaken or abandoned by the gods, Petr. poët. 124, 264.—Hence, mūtā-tus, a, um, P. a., changed, i. e. different, successive: quae (facies) mutatis inducitur atque fovetur Tot medicaminibus,.

mundus, a, um, adj.
Sanscr. mund, purificari
,
clean, cleanly, nice, neat, elegant.
Lit. (class.; syn.: lautus, nitidus, purus): supellex,: caena,: ager,: mundissimum cubile desiderat (animal),: jam intus mundissimumst,.—Poet., with abl., = ornatus: Ostia munita est: idem loca navibus pulchris Munda facit, adorned, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 146 Vahl.).—
Transf.
Of mode of living, neat, fine, elegant, smart, genteel: cultus justo mundior,too elegant dress,.— As subst.: mundus, i, m. (sc. homo), an elegant or nice person, .—
Of quality, not coarse, fine (post-class.): annonae, of wheat,: panis,.—
Trop.
Of speech, neat, fine, elegant (poet. and in postclass. prose): verba, Ov A. A. 3, 479: versus, quibus mundius nihil reperiri puto,: in Gallos mundius subtiliusque est, quam cum Gallis aut contra Gallos,—
Subst.: mun-dum, i. n., only in the phrase: in mundo (esse or habere), in readiness (ante-class.): tibi vita seu mors in mundo est, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 457 Vahl.: in mundo pro palam et in expedito ac cito, Charis.): nempe habeo in mundo,: mihi in mundo sunt virgae,; : nescio quid vero habeo in mundo,; Ritschl.—
In eccl. Lat., morally pure, upright, free from sin: cor mundum crea in me, Deus,: beati mundo corde,.—Hence, adv., in two forms (both, for the most part, anteand post-class.).—
mundē, cleanly, neatly, prettily: (copia) in suo quaeque loco sita munde,: verrite aedes, spargite munde, Titin. ap. P.: parum munde et parum decenter,: munde facti versus,: quam mundissime purissimeque fiat,.—
mun-dĭter, cleanly, neatly.
Lit.: cum sedulo munditer nos habeamus,.—
Trop., decently, with propriety: dicere,.

la:noun:mundus.gloss: universe, world, esp. the heavens and the heavenly bodies

la:noun:mundus.html:
mundus, i, m. (
neutr. collat. form, mundum: legavit quidam uxori mundum omne penumque, all her toilet, Lucil. ap. , and ap. ) [1. mundus], toilet ornaments, decorations, dress (of a woman).
Lit.: mundus muliebris est, quo mulier mundior fit: continentur eo specula, matulae, unguenta, vasa unguentaria, et si qua similia dici possunt, veluti lavatio, riscus ... Unguenta, quibus valetudinis causā unguimur, mundo non continentur,: munditiae et ornatus et cultus, haec feminarum insignia sunt: hunc mundum muliebrem appellārunt majores nostri,: virginalis, Att. ap. Paul. ex Müll.: quamvis auro, veste, gemmis, omnique cetero mundo exornata mulier incedat,. —
Transf.
In gen., an implement (ante- and post-class.): operae messoriae mundus,implements for the harvest work,: Cereris,the mystical casket of Ceres, (the expression in mundo esse and habere belongs to the adj. mundus, v. mundus, II. B.).—
Like the Gr. κόσμος, the universe, the world, esp. the heavens and the heavenly bodies: ut hunc hac varietate distinctum bene Graeci κόσμον, nos lucentem mundum nominaremus, the heavens, : nam quem κόσμος Graeci, nomine ornamenti appellaverunt. eum nos a perfectā absolutāque elegantiā, mundum, : concussit micantia sidera mundus, heaven shook, : aetherius,: arduus,: aestuat infelix angusto limite mundi,. Also: mundus caeli, Enn. ap. (Sat. v. 10, p. 156 Vahl.): o clarissima mundi Lumina,: immensi copia mundi,: ipse mundus deorum hominumque causā factus est...Est enim mundus quasi communis deorum atque hominum domus, aut urbs utrorumque,the world,: innumerabiles,: e tabulā pictos ediscere mundos,parts of the world,.—
Transf.
The world, i. e. the earth, the inhabitants of the earth, mankind (poet.): quicumque mundo terminus obstitit,: spes miseri mundi,; : fastos evolvere mundi,: mundum laedere,mankind,: nullā in parte mundi cessat ebrietas,; ; ; : (Alexander) scrutatur maria ignota, et, ut ita dicam, mundi claustra perrumpit,: mundi principio,.—
The heavens, i. e. the sky, the weather (post-class.): tepida indulget terris clementia mundi,: ad Eoos tractūs mundique teporem,.—
The sun (perh. only in Manilius): quā mundus redit,; .—
Euphemistically for the Lower World, the infernal regions. The opening into this mundus was at Rome, in the Comitium, and was kept covered with a stone (lapis manalis); three times in the year, on the 24th of August, the 5th of October, and the 8th of November, days sacred to the gods of the infernal regions, this round pit was opened, and all sorts of fruits were thrown into it as offerings, Varr. ap. ; Paul. ex Fest. s. v mundus, p. 154 Müll., and s. v. manalem lapidem, p. 128 ib.—
Esp. (eccl. Lat.), the world as opposed to the church; this world, the realm of sin and death, as opposed to Christ's kingdom of holiness and life: non pro mundo rogo,: de mundo non sunt,: princeps hujus mundi (i. e. Satan),; 14, 30: regnum meum non est de hoc mundo,; cf. ; .

mūnus (old orthogr. moenus;
moenera militiaï,), ĕris, n.
root mu-; cf.: moenia, munis, munia, etc.
, a service, office, post, employment, function, duty (class.; syn.: officium, ministerium, honos).
Lit.: munus significat officium, cum dicitur quis munere fungi. Item donum quod officii causā datur, Paul. ex Müll. (cf. infra): munus curare,to discharge an office,: octo munus hominum fungi,: administrare,: munus atque officium,: rei publicae,a public office,: belli,: de jure respondendi sustinere,: rei publicae explere,: vigiliarum obire,to perform,: officii,the performance of a duty,: tuum est hoc munus, tuae partes: a te hoc civitas exspectat,duty, office, obligation,: principum est resistere levitati multitudinis,: vitae,: senectutis,.—
Esp., = onus, a duty, burden, tribute: cum hoc munus imponebatur tam grave civitati,: id quoque munus leve atque commune Mamertinis remisisti,, § 52: dum ne quis eorum munere vacaret,: non enim detractionem eam munerum militiae, sed apertam defectionem esse,.—
Transf.
A work: majorum vigiliarum munus, prooem.: solitudinis,a work, book, written in solitude,.—
A service, favor: huc ire licet atque illuc munere ditium dominorum, Sall. Orat. Licin.; .—
In partic., the last service, office to the dead, i. e. burial: pro hominis dignitate amplo munere extulit, (dub.; al. funere): suprema,: supremum mortis,: debita,: fungi inani Munere,: cineri haec mittite nostro Munera,.—
A present, gift (syn.: donum, praemium): bonum datum deorum concessu atque munere,: mittere alicui,: mittere aliquid alicui munere,to send one something as a present, (al. muneri): quasi totam regionem muneri accepissent,had received as a present,: aliquem munere donare,to present one with a gift,: dare muneri aliquid alicui,to give one something as a present,: munera Liberi,i. e. wine,: terrae,: Cereris,bread,; cf.: gratae post munus aristae,: quem munere palpat Carus,i. e. a bribe,.—
In partic.
A public show, spectacle, entertainment, exhibition, esp. a show of gladiators, which was given to the people by the magistrates, and generally by the Ædiles, as an expression of gratitude for the honorable office to which they had been elected (cf.: ludus, spectaculum): erat munus Scipionis, dignum et eo ipso et illo Q. Metello, cui dabatur,: munus magnificum dare,: praebere,: functus est aedilicio maximo munere,i. e. gave a splendid exhibition,: edere,: venationes, quae vocantur munera,: munera nunc edunt,; .—
A public building for the use of the people, erected at the expense of an individual: Pompeii munera,the theatre,: aut ubi muneribus nati sua munera mater Addidit (i. e. theatro Marcelli porticum Octaviam),.—
Transf., of the structure of the universe: effector vel moderator tanti operis et muneris,.

la:adj:mutus.html:
mūtus, a, um, adj.
root mu-, to shut; Sanscr. mūkas, dumb; Gr. μύτις, μυάω; cf. Lat. mussare
,
dumb, mute (class.; cf.: infans, elinguis).
Lit., that does not speak, silent.—Of creatures who do not possess the faculty of speech, and can utter only inarticulate sounds: pecudes,: bestiae,: agna,: armenta,: animalia,: satius est mutum esse quam quod nemo intellegat dicere,: subjugale, animal, Pet. 2, 16: vere dici potest, magistratum legem esse loquentem, legem autem mutum magistratum,: papae! Jugularas hominem: quid ille? Thr. Mutus illico, he was struck speechless, was silent, could not say a word more, : ad mandata mancus est, caecus, mutus,: mutum dices, you shall call me dumb, i. e. I will not say a word, : omnis pro nobis gratia muta fuit,has not spoken a word,: mutus aspectus miserorum lacrimas movet,: numquam vox est de te mea muta,i. e. I have never ceased to praise thee,: dolore lyra est,: spiritus,which makes one mute,; .—Of that which utters no sound, dumb, mute, silent: tintinnabulum,: imago,: mare,the silent sea,: consonantes,which cannot be pronounced alone, mutes,: artes, the plastic arts, arts of design, opp. to eloquence, ; also, artes, the silent arts, i. e. which do not concern themselves with language, as medicine, : scientia,i. e. which does not impart the power of speaking,: instrumentum fundi,i. e. wagons, carts,: magistri,i. e. books,: lapides,that say nothing, have no inscriptions on them, Goes.: muta exta dicuntur, quibus nihil divinationis aut deorum responsi inesse animadvertunt, contra adjutoria, quae certum aliquid eventurum indicant, Paul. ex Müll.: simulacra muta,dumb idols,.—
Transf., of places where no sound is heard, silent, still: mutum forum, elinguem curiam, tacitam et fractam civitatem videbatis,: solitudo,: spelunca,.—Of times: nullum fuit tempus, quod magis debuerit mutum esse a litteris,in which nothing should have been written,: silentia noctis,the deep silence of night,.—Of things of which nothing is said: mutum aevum,not celebrated, unsung,.—As subst.

mūtum, i, n. (sc. animal), a dumb creature, brute: separat hoc nos A grege mutorum,.

senses: in return, in exchange, mutual, reciprocal
la:adj:mutuus.html:
mūtŭus, a, um, adj.
1. muto
,
borrowed, lent (class.).
Lit.: nullus est tibi, quem roges mutuom Argentum,to lend you money,; : mutuum talentum dare,to lend, advance,: mutuum argentum quaerere,to seek to borrow money,: huic drachmarum argenti haec mille dederat mutuom,: nam si mutuas (sc. minas) non potero, certumst sumam faenore,: mutuas pecunias sumere ab aliquo, to borrow or raise money of any one, : mutuum frumentum dare,to lend,: si quoi mutuom quid dederis, fit pro proprio perditum,.—
Subst.: mūtŭum, i, n., a loan: mutui datio,a lending,; .—In dat.: mutuo, by or upon a loan: aut sumtum aliunde, ut mutuo, aut factum ab ipso,: petere mutuo naves, pecuniam,: mutuo sumamus pecunias in tributa regis, Esdr. 5, 4; cf. adv. mutuo, infra; and Krebs, Antibarb. p. 731.—
Trop.: si pudoris egeas, sumas mutuum,borrow shame, if you have none,: ego cum illā facere nolo mutuum: Pa. Quid ita? Ph. Quia proprium facio; amo pariter semul,i. e. I do not want to borrow her love, but to possess it as my own,.—
Transf., in return, in exchange, reciprocal, mutual: olores mutuā carne vescuntur inter se,eat one another,: funera,: vulnera,wounds inflicted by each on the other,: officia,: aemulatio virtutis,: nox omnia erroris mutui implevit,on both sides,: odia,: accusatio,: mutuum facere,to do the same, return like for like,: ut amore perdita est haec misera! Pyr. Mutuum fit (sc. a me), I do the same, return like for like, : per mutua, mutually, on or from one another: pedibus per mutua nexis,. So, mutua: inter se mortales mutua vivunt,: e laevo sit mutua dexter,again, on the other hand, (302): mutuus ut nos Affectus petere auxilium juberet,: —Hence, adv., in three forms.
mū-tŭō, in return, by turns, reciprocally, mutually (class.; cf.: invicem, vicissim): studia officii mutuo inter nos certatim constiterunt, Lepid. ap. : me mutuo diligas, Planc. ap. : exercere officia cum multis,: cum de se mutuo sentire provinciam crederet, that it was disposed towards him as he was towards it, Auct. B. Alex. 48.—
mūtŭē, mutually, in return (class.): respondere, (al. mutuo): respondisse, (al. mutuo).—
mūtŭĭter, mutually, in return (anteclass.): vive, meque ama mutuiter, Varr. ap. .

la:adj:muliebris.html:
mŭlĭĕbris, e, adj.
mulier
,
of or belonging to a woman, womanly, female, feminine.
Adj. (class.): loci muliebres, ubi nascendi initia consistunt,: facinus,: comitatus,: vox,: vestis,: venustas,: fraus,: impotentia,: certamen, i. e. de mulieribus,: jura,: Fortuna Muliebris, worshipped in memory of the wife and mother of Coriolanus, who persuaded him to retreat,; .—
In a reproachful sense, womanish, effeminate, unmanly: parce muliebri supellectili. Mi. Quae ea est supellex? Ha. Clarus clamor sine modo, : animum geritis muliebrem, Poët. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 227 Rib.): muliebris enervataque sententia,.—Gram. t. t., feminine (opp. virilis): vocabulum, Müll.—
Subst.: mŭlĭĕbrĭa, ĭum, n.
= pu denda muliebria, : muliebria pati,to let one's self be used as a woman,.—
Womanish things: muliebria cetera, = menstrua: desierant Sarae fieri muliebria,.—Hence, adv.: mŭlĭĕ-brĭter.
In the manner of a woman, like a woman: nec muliebriter Expavit ensem,: ingemiscens,: flere,: Hunni equis muliebriter insidentes,in the manner of women,.—
Womanishly, effeminately: si se lamentis muliebriter lacrimisque dedet. : ne quid serviliter muliebriterve faciamus,: Antinăum suum muliebriter flere,.

la:noun:musa.html:
Mūsa, ae, f., = Μοῦσα,
a muse, one of the goddesses of poetry, music, and the other liberal arts. The ancients reckoned nine of them, viz.: Clio, the muse of history; Melpomene, of tragedy; Thalia, of comedy; Euterpe, of the flute; Terpsichore, of dancing; Calliope, of epic poetry; Erato, of lyric poetry; Urania, of astronomy; Polyhymnia, of the mimic art, ; ; : Musarum delubra,: hic Musarum parens domusque Pieria, Mela, 2, 3, 2: crassiore Musā,in a plainer, clearer manner, without too much refinement,: sine ullā Musā, without any genius, wit, taste, Varr. ap. .—
Transf.
A song, a poem: musa procax,: pedestris,a style of poetry bordering on prose,.—
Plur., sciences, studies: quis est omnium, qui modo cum Musis, id est cum humanitate et cum doctrinā habeat aliquod commercium, qui, etc.,: agrestiores,: mansuetiores,philosophical studies,.

la:verb:munio.gloss: to provide with defensive works, fortify
senses: to provide with defensive works, fortify
to safeguard, uphold or buttress (of a person, institution, etc.)
to build up so as to give a firm surface to, to construct or repair (of a road, other raised areas)
la:verb:munio.html:
mūnĭo (old form moenio, v. below), īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4 (
fut. munibis for munies, ), v. a.
moenia, lit. to wall; hence
, to build a wall around, to defend with a wall, to fortify, defend, protect, secure, put in a state of defence (class.).
Lit.: arcem ad urbem obsidendam,: palatium,: locum,.—With abl.: Alpibus Italiam munierat ante natura,: domum praesidiis,: castra vallo fossāque,with palisades and a trench,: locum muro,.—With a homogeneous object, prov.: magna moenis moenia,you are undertaking a great thing,: duovir urbis moeniendae,.— Absol.: quod idoneum ad muniendum putarent, for fortifying, i. e. for use in the fortifications, ; . —Also, to surround, guard, for the protection of other things: ignem ita munire ut non evagaretur, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 12, 7, 7.—
Transf.
In gen., to defend, guard, secure, protect, shelter: Pergamum divinā moenitum manu,: hortum ab incursu hominum,: spica contra avium morsūs munitur vallo aristarum,: hieme quaternis tunicis et tibialibus muniebatur,he defended, protected, covered himself,. —
To make a road, etc., i. e. to make passable by opening, repairing, or paving it: quasi Appius Caecus viam munierit,: rupem,: itinera,: TEMPE MVNIVIT,. —
Trop.
To guard, secure, strengthen, support (cf.: fulcio, sustineo): meretriculis Muniendis rem cogere,to maintain, support, (dub.; Speng. moenerandis; v. munero).—Am strengthening myself: munio me ad haec tempora,: imperium,to secure,: muniri adversus fraudes,to secure one's self, (dub. moneri, Jahn): se contra ruborem,: se multorum benevolentiā,: se contra perfidiam,: aliquid auctoritate,: domum terrore,.—
Munire viam, to make or open a way: haec omnia tibi accusandi viam muniebant,prepared the way for your accusation,: sibi viam ad stuprum,.—Hence, mūnītus, a, um, P. a., defended, fortified, protected, secured, safe (class.): nullius pudicitia munita contra tuam cupiditatem et audaciam posset esse,.—Neutr. plur. munita as subst.: munita viāi, fortification or breastwork of the mouth (cf. Homer. ἕρκος ὀδόντων), the lips, .—Comp.: se munitiorem ad custodiendam vitam suam fore,.—Sup.: munitissima castra,.—Adv.: mūnītē, securely, safely (ante-class.): munitius,. Müll.

la:noun:munditia.html:
mundĭtĭa, ae, and mundĭtĭes, ēi, f.
1. mundus
,

Lit.: munditia illecebra animo est amantium,: munditias facere,to clean the house,: munditias volo fieri; ecferte huc scopas, etc.,: alia jam munditiarum facies est,.—
Transf., in gen., cleanliness, neatness, elegance, fineness, niceness, in furniture, dress, etc.: in munditiis aetatulam agere,: munditiis munditiam antideo,: munditia non odiosa neque exquisita nimis,: hominis,: cui flavam religas comam, Simplex munditiis,: munditiis capimur,: urbanae,: per cultum et munditias,: multa munditia indutus et amictus,. —
Trop., of speech, neatness, terseness, elegance, : verborum,: venustas et mundities orationis,; .

In partic., in arithmetic, to multiply: multiplicantur in se duo latera,: has duas summas in se multiplicato,: latitudinis pedes cum longitudinis pedibus sic multiplicabis,: ter tria,: annos quater, dies octies,; .

4: legatus muneratus,.—In gerundive: non meretriculis moenerandis rem coëgit, Speng.— Absol.: at certatim nutricant et munerant,: regni eum societate muneravit,: dignus quem maximis officiis muneres,. —

mūtĭo or muttĭo, īvi, 4, v. n.
from the sound mu

to mutter, mumble, speak in a low tone (poet.; syn.: murmuro, musso).
Lit.: etiam muttis? So. Jam tacebo, ; : inpinge pugnum, si muttiverit,; : nihil jam mutire audeo,: neque opus est Adeo mutito,nor should it even be muttered, be hinted at,: si muttivero, etiam quod certo scio,.—

To bleat, as a he-goat, Auct. Carm. Philom. 58; to bark: non mutiet canis,.—
To creak, of a hinge: num muttit cardo?.—
Mutire, loqui. Ennius in Telepho: palam mutire plebeio piaculum est, Paul. ex Müll. (Trag. v. 376 Vahl.).

la:noun:murmur.html:
murmur, ŭris, n. (m.: murmur fit verus, Varr. ap. ) [Sanscr. marmara, susurrus, murmur, and the Greek μορμύρω and μυρμύρω],
a murmur, murmuring; a humming, roaring, growling, grumbling; a rushing, crashing, etc. (class.; syn.: fremitus, strepitus, fragor, stridor, susurrus): murmur populi,: serpitque per agmina murmur. : quanto porrexit murmure panem,.—Of prayer, a low, indistinct tone: quos ubi placavit precibus et murmure longo,; .—Of the humming of bees: strepit omnis murmure campus,.—Of the roar of a lion, ; of the tiger: tigridis Hyrcanae jejunum murmur,.—Of inanimate things, a murmur, roar, rushing, crashing, crash, rumbling: nam et odor urbanitatis, et mollitudo humanitatis, et murmur maris, et dulcedo orationis sunt ducta a ceteris sensibus,: dare,to roar,: magno misceri murmure caelum,: ventosum,the rushing wind,.—Of thunder: exanimes primo murmure caeli,.—Of a volcanic mountain: Aetnaei verticis,.—Of an earthquake, a roaring, rumbling: praecedit sonus, alias murmuri similis, alias mugitibus, aut clamori humano, armorumve pulsantium fragori,.—Of wind-instruments: cornuum,the sound,: inflati buxi, of the tibia, : aurium,a singing in the ears, (Jahn, animalia).—Trop.: contemnere murmura famae,; of a muttering, rebellious murmur: contra Dominum,; .

senses: to stroke, graze, touch lightly or gently
la:verb:mulceo.html:
mulcĕo, si, sum (rarely mulctum), 2, v. a.
Sanscr. root marc, take hold of; Gr. μάρπτω, μάρπτις; cf. mulco
,

Lit.: manu mulcens barbam,: caput,: vitulum,: colla,: mulcebant Zephyri flores,rustle through,: aura mulcet rosas,virgā mulcere capillos,to touch lightly,: aristas,: mulcere alternos (pueros) et corpora fingere linguā,: aëra motu,: aethera pennis,to move,: mulserat huc navem compulsam fluctibu' pontus, had wafted hither, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 257 Vahl.).—
Transf., to make sweet or pleasant: pocula succis Lyaei,. —
Trop., to soothe, soften, appease, allay; to caress, flatter, delight, etc. (syn.: blandior. placo, lenio, sedo): mulcentem tigres, of Orpheus,: aliquem dictis,: fluctūs,: iras,: jure,.—To alleviate, mitigate: variā vulnera mulcet ope,alleviates the pain of his wounds,: dolores nervorum,: os stomachumque,: ebrietatem,: lassitudinem,: corpora fessa,: aliquem laudibus, to flatter, Pac. ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. Mulciber, p. 144 Müll. (Trag. Rel. p. 109 Rib.): puellas carmine,to delight,: animos admiratione,: aures figmentis verborum novis,to delight,.—Hence, mulsus, a, um, P. a.
Adj., mixed with honey; sweet as honey, honey-sweet (post-Aug.): mulsa (sc. aqua),honey-water, hydromel,: acetum,vinegar and honey mixed together, honey-vinegar,: lac,: mulsa pira,.— Trop., of words, etc., sweet as honey, honeyed (Plautin.): ut mulsa dicta dicis!: loqui,.—
Subst.
mulsa, ae, f., a term of endearment, my sweetheart, my honey (Plautin.): age, mulsa mea,; .—
mulsum, i, n. (sc. vinum), honey-wine, mead, i. e. wine mixed or made with honey (class.): commisce mulsum,; : frigidum,: aceti, for mulsum acetum,honeyvinegar,.

moirus,), i, m.

, a wall; esp. a city wall; mostly in plur. (class.; cf.: moenia, paries, maceria).
